name: Almond oil / castor oil

card.summary: Plant oils massaged under the eyes for dark circles and fine lines; widely used as cosmetic carriers, but untested for this purpose.
card.aka: Sweet almond oil, Ricinus communis oil
card.note: Nut allergy applies to almond oil; keep oils away from the eye itself.

quick.overview:
Sweet almond oil and castor oil are massaged around the eyes by people hoping to moisturise, lighten dark circles or soften lines. Both are common cosmetic ingredients.

No clinical study of either oil for under-eye appearance was found.
quick.mechanism: Both oils are emollients. Almond oil is mostly oleic and linoleic acid with vitamin E; castor oil is about 90 percent ricinoleate. Proponents credit them with nourishing the skin, but effects on dark circles have not been tested.
quick.risks: Almonds can cause allergy, from oral allergy syndrome to anaphylaxis, though reference sources do not address the oil specifically. Bitter almond oil is a different product containing benzaldehyde. Oils near the eye can cause irritation or blurred vision.

lead: Almond oil and castor oil are plant oils that people massage into the skin around the eyes to moisturise thin eyelid skin, soften the look of fine lines and, as proponents hope, lighten dark circles. Castor oil is also widely applied to eyebrows and eyelashes by people who want fuller-looking brows and lashes, which makes it one of the more discussed oils on looksmaxxing forums.

Sweet almond oil is a common cosmetic carrier oil; about 70 percent of its fat is monounsaturated, mainly oleic acid, and it contains vitamin E.[1] Castor oil is pressed from Ricinus communis seeds, and about 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleates; it is used as a moisturiser in creams.[2] A 2017 review of topical plant oils, almond oil among them, describes anti-inflammatory and skin-barrier-repair effects reported for oils applied to skin.[3]

No clinical trial of either oil applied under the eyes or to brows and lashes for appearance was found. Reference sources describe general cosmetic use, and forum users report mixed personal results for castor oil on brows and lashes.[1][2][4][6]

chain: Oil is massaged under the eyes or brushed onto brows and lashes
The emollient coats and softens skin and hair
Skin looks more moisturised; users hope for fuller brows and lashes
angle.text: People gently massage a small amount of oil around the eye area to soften and moisturise the skin, and brush castor oil onto brows and lashes with a small brush. The goals are a smoother, more hydrated under-eye look and thicker-looking brows and lashes. Reported results vary between users.

infobox: Mostly oleic and linoleic acids; vitamin E [1]
Under-eye massage, brows, lashes, general moisturising
None found for these appearance uses

paras: Almond oil is pressed from sweet or bitter almond kernels; the sweet type is the cosmetic carrier oil, while bitter almond oil contains benzaldehyde and is used for flavouring and perfume.[1] Castor oil's polar ricinoleic acid makes it unusual among vegetable oils.[2]

Proponents say regular gentle massage with either oil nourishes thin eyelid skin and lightens circles. Reference articles describe the oils' general cosmetic and moisturising roles and do not report appearance outcomes for the eye area.[1][2] A review of plant oils applied to skin describes anti-inflammatory and barrier-repair effects for several oils including almond oil, in work not specific to dark circles.[3]

On looksmax.org, castor oil is discussed mainly as a brow and lash product, applied with a small brush. One user reported a month of nightly use and said a friend noticed thicker lashes, adding that brow colour changed little.[6] Others report barely noticeable difference after a year, including when combined with minoxidil on brows, and say a prescription lash product did more.[4] A further thread asks about castor oil mixed with rosemary oil, with one reply saying the evidence is not strong but that the oil also acts a bit like mascara.[5]

Almonds can cause allergy and intolerance with cross-reactivity to other tree nuts and peach allergens.[1] Castor oil is regarded as non-toxic after processing because heating during extraction deactivates ricin.[2] A toxicology review reports that absorption of ricin, a seed protein, through intact skin is most unlikely.[7] Oils placed close to the eye can cause irritation or blurred vision.

Reviews have looked at castor oil in eye-surface conditions such as blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction and dry eye, which are medical rather than cosmetic topics.[8] A randomised trial in healthy Asian women found that eating almonds increased the skin's UVB resistance; this concerned dietary almonds, not the oil.[9]

No studies found for either oil used under the eyes or on brows and lashes for appearance. Related research covers plant oils for skin-barrier repair in general,[3] castor oil for eye-surface conditions,[8] and dietary almonds and UV resistance.[9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, castor oil is a frequent topic for brows and lashes, with some users reporting visible results and others little change; almond oil appears far less often.

claims.believers: One user posted that after about a month of nightly use the lashes grew noticeably and a friend saw better thickness.[6]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested castor oil for eyelash or eyebrow growth.

claims.claim: Castor oil barely does anything for brows
claims.believers: Other users report barely noticeable change after a year, including alongside minoxidil, and say Latisse did more for lashes and brows.[4]
claims.experts: No published human trial has compared castor oil with these products for brows.

claims.claim: Castor oil with rosemary oil helps brows and lashes
claims.believers: A thread asks whether the combination is worthwhile, with replies saying it is a reasonable add-on and that it can coat hairs like mascara.[5]
claims.experts: No published studies were found of this combination for brow or lash growth.

claims.claim: Oils under the eyes soften dark circles and fine lines
claims.believers: Proponents say gentle massage nourishes the thin skin and lightens circles.
claims.experts: Reference sources describe the oils as emollients; no trial of either oil for dark circles was found.[1][2]
